segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of Charles Dickens's great fog-bound novel.
Each episode we take a handful of passages and ask what Dickens is really doing — with his language, his characters, his moral world.
I'm joined today by three guests whose company I trust absolutely when it comes to this novel.
First, Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, formidable literary conscience, and a reader who insists that great fiction is ultimately about moral character, not social programme.
Edmund brings the kind of patience and precision that Bleak House rewards above almost any other novel.
Second, Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has given more classic novels their voices on audio than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver hears Dickens as a performer — the comic timing, the rhythms, the moments written for the voice rather than the page.
And third, Caroline Woodcourt — book critic, devoted re-reader of this novel, and someone who cares deeply about what the experience of reading Bleak House actually feels like, sentence by sentence.
Today we begin where Dickens begins — with atmosphere, with fog, with the strange moral climate this novel breathes.
What strikes me every time I return to Bleak House is that Dickens is building a world that is almost entirely composed of distortion.
Not just the fog of the opening chapters — though that is extraordinary — but distortion right down into the family, into childhood itself.
There is a passage about the Smallweed family that I find genuinely alarming — and absolutely hilarious — in equal measure.
Dickens describes how this family has, over generations, systematically eradicated every trace of play, of story, of imagination from its children.
He writes that the house of Smallweed has — and I must read this properly —
"discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities whatsoever."
And the consequence — delivered with that magnificent straight face —
"the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds."
"Something depressing on their minds" — that is one of the great comic phrases in English literature.
What I love about that passage is how the comedy and the horror are genuinely inseparable.
Dickens is describing the deliberate murder of childhood — of fairy-tales, of fictions — and calling the result gratifying.
That word — gratifying — carries all the weight of the society that produced the Smallweeds.
And then that image of the monkeys — it's appalling and funny all at once.
But what lingers, when you stop laughing, is the phrase Oliver just read — "no child born to it."
The Smallweeds have abolished childhood so thoroughly that in some real sense they have abolished children altogether.
I take Caroline's point, and I would not diminish the satirical ferocity there.
But I think we must also ask what Dickens places against the Smallweed world — and it is, in this novel, something altogether grander.
Consider what Mr. Bucket does in the closing movements of this book — not as a function of plot, but as a human being.
He reconciles a mother and her son with a warmth and directness that is genuinely touching.
And then he turns to Sir Leicester Dedlock and makes what I can only call a vow — and it is worth hearing precisely.
"Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, what you've trusted to me I'll go through with.
Don't you be afraid of my turning out of my way, right or left, or taking a sleep, or a wash, or a shave till I have found what I go in search of."
There is a moral seriousness in that speech — a personal honour — that no satire can dissolve.
Edmund is right about Bucket — and what's remarkable as a performer is that Dickens gives him both registers at once.
That speech has comedy in it — "a wash, or a shave" — and yet it is completely, utterly sincere.
Dickens trusts the reader not to laugh it away.
And that sincerity is all the more powerful when you set it against the scene that follows — the great house at night.
George Rouncewell walking through Chesney Wold — holding up his light — thinking of Lady Dedlock, of Tulkinghorn, of the master upstairs who doesn't yet know.
Dickens writes that George reflects how he might see something now which it would tax his boldness to approach.
"he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy.
But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
Blank — repeated, and earned.
That blankness is not nihilism — I want to be precise about this.
It is the silence that precedes — and perhaps enables — moral reckoning.
Chesney Wold is blank because the people who gave it meaning — who gave duty and loyalty their shape — are absent or broken.
And what Dickens is asking, I think, is whether those things can be recovered — whether people like George, like Bucket, can recover them.
Fog and blankness as the condition from which character — and conscience — must emerge.
That is a rich foundation, and it's exactly where we'll dig deeper in the segments to come.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're diving into one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs — the slow unmaking of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins as one of the most appealing young men in all of Dickens — spirited, generous, full of promise.
And the novel proceeds, with terrible patience, to dismantle him.
With me to take this apart are Edmund Leigh, Caroline Woodcourt, and Oliver Trevelyan.
Edmund brings his unfailing eye for moral character — and for what Dickens really asks of his young men.
Caroline has lived with this novel long enough to feel every stage of Richard's decline as a personal loss.
And Oliver, who has voiced Richard in more than one recorded edition, knows this young man from the inside.
Let's start at a moment that looks, on its surface, like hope.
What strikes me most about these early chapters is that Richard is not yet lost — he is merely untested.
And the scene in which he and Ada confide their love to Esther is, in its way, entirely charming.
Esther's account of it is beautifully observed — she tells us she never stopped their wild, rapturous talk.
"I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That is Esther at her most warm and self-aware — fully present, fully fond.
But Dickens embeds the caution immediately within the tenderness.
Love, Esther tells them, can only come to happiness if it inspires constancy, fortitude, and perseverance.
Three words — and each one, in the end, will be precisely what Richard fails.
Edmund's right about those three words — they land like a sentence handed down before the crime is committed.
And what I keep returning to is the visual image Dickens gives us at the close of that chapter.
Esther and Mr. Jarndyce watch Richard and Ada walk away through the sunlit rooms.
"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come."
It is glorious — and then it turns.
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
One sentence.
"The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Dickens doesn't reach for that effect — he simply describes what the room does, and it destroys you.
Caroline, when I first read that passage aloud — in a studio, entirely alone — I had to stop.
Because you cannot perform those final sentences.
Any emphasis you add is wrong — the text does it all.
But what I find equally devastating is what Mr. Jarndyce says to Richard in the scene before that passage.
He's giving the boy the formula for a decent life — as plainly and generously as a man can.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that is wonderful.
A man who prays for his cart to be lifted from the mud but never puts his shoulder to the wheel.
That is Richard in miniature — and Jarndyce sees it coming before Richard has even begun.
Oliver touches on something I think is absolutely central to the moral architecture of this novel.
Jarndyce is not lecturing Richard — he is making a covenant with him.
He says, in effect: I will not presume to predict your future, I will not be your judge — I will only remain your friend.
"If you DO change — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
The word 'monstrous' is key — Jarndyce anticipates not simply failure but shame, and tries to disarm it in advance.
Richard's tragedy is not that he lacks good counsel — it is that he cannot receive it.
And that is a failure of character, not of circumstance.
I want to push on that slightly — because Dickens also builds in a structural trap for Richard.
It isn't only that Richard drifts — every institution he enters turns out to be the wrong fit.
And Mrs. Badger — marvellous, precise Mrs. Badger — names the problem with medicine exactly.
She says that Richard finds medicine a tiresome pursuit — that he has not the positive interest that makes it a vocation.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
That contrast with Woodcourt is quietly ruthless.
Woodcourt will be everything Richard cannot be — and they are set in orbit around the same woman.
Mrs. Badger is one of those comic characters who earns her keep by saying the truest thing in the scene.
She floats in on a cloud of her late husbands — the distinguished Captain Swosser, the celebrated Professor Dingo — and then delivers a verdict of clinical precision.
Richard, she says, will never find medicine anything but tiresome.
And she is right — as she is always right — while somehow remaining entirely delightful.
The comedy and the tragedy are wound together so tightly in Dickens that you can't pull them apart.
Mrs. Badger is funny — and Richard's fate is already sealed.
Caroline asks whether it is truly a failure of character or a structural trap — and I think Dickens offers us both, without fully resolving the question.
Jarndyce, in the earlier passage, reaches back to remember how he once imagined Richard and Ada together — afar off, he says.
"I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
The repetition of 'afar off' is not rhetoric — it is anxiety.
Jarndyce knows — has perhaps always known — that the distance between what Richard is and what he needs to become is very great indeed.
And that distance, of course, is what the novel will spend so many chapters measuring — fathom by fathom.
Edmund, Caroline, Oliver — thank you.
When we return, we'll be looking at the fog — that great enveloping presence that opens the novel and never really lifts.

segments.title: Secrets and Lies: Lady Dedlock's Web

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's most compulsive and dangerous relationships — the silent war between Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn.
And beneath that war, the buried secret of Esther Summerson's origins — slowly coming to light through the most carefully guarded disclosure in Victorian fiction.
With me are Sir Edmund Leigh, who will remind us that moral imagination is at stake here, not merely plot mechanics.
Oliver Trevelyan, who has voiced both Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock across separate productions and knows these characters from the inside.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has strong feelings — I suspect — about what Esther deserves to know, and when.
Edmund, let's begin with you — with the scene at the heart of this web, where Dickens shows us the extraordinary poker match between these two.
What strikes me first, and most forcibly, is Dickens's absolute command of what we might call the drama of restraint.
He is not showing us people who lose control — he is showing us people of formidable will who keep it, at tremendous cost.
The passage describing this particular exchange is almost unbearably precise in its observations.
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."
That phrase — without any other alteration in their customary deportment — is doing extraordinary work.
The surface is perfectly maintained — and that perfect maintenance is itself the most eloquent sign of danger.
Meanwhile, poor Sir Leicester gazes at the fire, entirely oblivious — Dickens places him there with devastating economy.
Edmund's absolutely right about Sir Leicester and the fire — it's one of those moments where Dickens tells you everything with one gesture.
The man looks at the fire, with — and I love this — with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.
He's a portrait of himself, essentially — decorative, ancestral, and entirely unaware of the crisis unfolding three feet away.
But when I think about performing these scenes, what grips me is the passage where they meet again, day after day, and neither blinks.
Dickens builds the tension across repeated encounters with this extraordinary description — let me read it properly.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
Exhausted deity — it's a phrase that contains an entire social world in three words.
And it tells you exactly how to play her: the boredom is not affectation — it is the armour she lives inside.
What I keep returning to in that passage is the symmetry Dickens constructs between them.
She is the exhausted deity; he is the speechless repository of noble confidences — so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.
Two people in disguise, essentially — each performing a social role that conceals their actual power.
And then Dickens pulls back to give us that great accumulating question — the one that runs like a buried current through the whole novel.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
What each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.
For the time — those three words are doing all the work.
They are a promise, and a warning, and a perfectly placed dread.
Caroline has identified something I think is essential — this is not merely suspense as mechanism.
It is, at the deepest level, a study in the moral cost of secrecy — in what it does to a person to live perpetually in concealment.
Lady Dedlock has constructed this persona — this deity, as Oliver rightly called her — over a past that she has buried alive.
And that buried thing is not merely a biographical fact — it is a human being.

The chapter in which Jarndyce finally tells Esther what he knows — what little he was ever permitted to know — is extraordinarily moving precisely because it reveals how much was concealed even from him.
The letter, he tells her, was written with a stern passion and power that rendered it unlike all other letters I have ever read.
"It was written to me, perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it."
The grammar of that sentence enacts the very thing it describes — a trust extended with extraordinary delicacy, and an acceptance equally careful.
And what that letter actually contained — when Jarndyce reports it — stops you cold.
He's speaking directly to Esther, remember — this is the moment when she learns she was not simply unfortunate, but systematically erased.
The letter told him that the writer had bred her in secrecy from her birth, and — and this is the phrase that stays with me — had blotted out all trace of her existence.

"It told me that the writer had bred her in secrecy from her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence, and that if the writer were to die before the child became a woman, she would be left entirely friendless, nameless, and unknown."
Friendless, nameless, and unknown — three words, three death blows.
Dickens knows exactly when to let the plainest language carry the heaviest freight.
And then there is the religious dimension — which I find one of the most disturbing things in this entire strand of the novel.
Because it is not enough that Esther has been hidden — she has been made to feel guilty for her own existence.
Jarndyce describes this with a kind of controlled horror — the distorted religion which clouded her mind.
"The distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent."
Quite innocent — and yet made to carry it.
The cruelty here isn't external — it has been internalised, made doctrine, made theology.
And we understand, reading this, exactly the weight that Esther carries throughout the whole novel without ever quite naming its source.
I would not disagree with a syllable of that — and yet I'd add one further note.
The mother's resolution to maintain secrecy — even through her intermediary, even at such cost to herself and to Esther — is not simply cruel.
It is, as Jarndyce puts it, the product of an absolutely steadfast will — almost tragic in its consistency.
He tells Esther that more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
That phrase, for any human consideration, is the measure of what we are dealing with — a will that has placed itself beyond ordinary human appeal.
Whether one calls that strength or catastrophic pride depends, I think, on where one's sympathies finally lie.
And that is precisely the question the novel refuses to settle — which is why Lady Dedlock haunts us rather than merely troubles us.
She assumes a false name; she claims only the most minimal relation — the child's aunt, not mother; she discloses only enough to ensure the child's survival.
It is, depending on how you read it, either the most she could do or the least she could get away with.
And Dickens — characteristically — gives us both readings simultaneously.

What this conversation has illuminated for me is how Dickens makes secrecy itself a structural force in the novel — not just a plot device, but a kind of moral gravity pulling everything towards revelation.
Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn locked in mutual surveillance; Esther unknowingly carrying a history that was blotted out before she could speak; Jarndyce trusted with just enough to act, and no more.
In our next segment, we turn to the fog — literal and moral — that Dickens throws over all of this: Chancery, the law, and the great grinding mechanism that implicates everyone.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the series where we sit with Dickens's great novel and try to understand what makes it so extraordinary.
I'm joined today by Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and one of the finest close readers of Victorian fiction alive.
By Oliver Trevelyan, actor, writer, and the man who has lent his voice to more classic novels than anyone breathing.
And by Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and a reader who has lived inside Bleak House since her teenage years.
Today's segment is called The Savage and the Genteel — and we're looking at two worlds Dickens places directly beside each other in these chapters.
On one side, Jo — the crossing-sweeper, illiterate, destitute, barely human in the eyes of respectable society.
On the other, Lord Boodle and Sir Leicester Dedlock, discussing the affairs of the nation over dinner.
Caroline, shall we begin with Jo? Because Dickens does something almost unbearable in these passages.
He does something that I think is almost technically impossible — he makes the inarticulate eloquent.
Jo has no education, no language for grief, no words that would be recognised in a drawing room.
And yet when he speaks of the man who was kind to him, Nemo, you are simply undone.
The passage reads, and I want everyone to hear this properly —
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
Six words — and the repetition at the end, that second 'he wos,' that's not padding.
That's a child trying to make himself believed, because no one in his world ever believes him about anything.
And the spelling, Caroline — Dickens spells it as Jo speaks it.
'Wery.' 'Wos.' 'Stritched.'
On the page those spellings look almost comic — almost music-hall.
But spoken aloud, with the boy wiping his eyes on his wretched sleeve, they become the saddest sounds in the book.
I have read Jo's lines many times in recording studios — and I've never once got through them without feeling the room change.
What strikes me — and I think this is Dickens at his most morally serious — is that Jo's tribute to Nemo is completely without self-pity.
The boy grieves for the man, not for himself. That is the precise inversion of sentimentality.
And Dickens compounds it in the next passage — Jo comes to the cemetery at night, alone, and simply does what little he can.
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
That word 'softly' — in a description of sweeping a graveyard step — is almost unbearable in its precision.
The boy cannot speak a eulogy. He cannot leave flowers. He sweeps.
And notice how Dickens describes Jo in that cemetery passage — not as 'he' but as 'it.'
'With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate.'
A 'figure.' A 'slouching figure.' Not a boy. Not a person.
Dickens is showing us how society sees Jo — as an 'it' — and then demolishing that view in the very same sentence.
Because this 'it' holds the gate gently. This 'it' looks in. This 'it' cleans the step of a man it loved.
Which makes what follows — Lord Boodle at Sir Leicester's dinner table — almost funny in its grotesquerie.
Almost. Because by the time you've spent time with Jo, the comedy has a very sharp edge.
Lord Boodle is very worried about the nation. Very worried indeed.
The crisis, as he explains to Sir Leicester, is this —
"What are you to do with Noodle? You can't offer him the Presidency of the Council; that is reserved for Poodle."
Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle, Hoodle — Dickens just keeps going, and the longer it goes the funnier and the angrier it gets.
These are the men who run England, and the only question that exercises them is which of their Noodles gets which sinecure.
I confess I resist the temptation to make this purely political — Dickens is not writing a pamphlet.
But the structural juxtaposition is undeniable and, I think, entirely intentional.
The boy who cannot be provided for — not because there is no office to give him, but because he does not exist in the political imagination at all.
And then the punchline Dickens delivers with perfectly controlled fury —
"That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The country is not shipwrecked because Jo has no food, no shelter, no name in the eyes of the law.
It is shipwrecked, apparently, because Noodle has not been given a sufficiently prestigious desk.
And there is the hinge of the whole segment — the comparison Dickens doesn't make explicit, but doesn't need to.
Jo sweeps a dead man's step in the dark because it is the only thing he can offer.
Lord Boodle worries that there is no cabinet post grand enough for Noodle.
Dickens places those two images side by side, and trusts us to feel what he will not say.
After the break, we'll move deeper into the fog — and the question of what Bleak House itself means.

segments.title: The Court of Chancery: Dickens's Machinery of Madness

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great fog-shrouded novel apart — very carefully — to see what's inside.
I'm your host, and today we're beginning at the beginning — with the Court of Chancery and Dickens's extraordinary machinery of institutional madness.
With me are three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing something quite different to the table.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose approach to fiction is rigorously moral — he reads novels as stories about character tested by circumstance, not as political manifestos.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novel audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he comes to Dickens as a performer first — hearing the rhythms, catching the comic timing.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since — she reads with her whole heart.
Edmund, the novel opens with fog — quite literally, fog — and I'd like to start there.
What is Dickens doing with that extraordinary opening passage?
It is, I think, one of the most audacious opening gambits in all of English prose fiction.
Dickens does not ease us in. He does not set a scene in the conventional sense. He detonates one.
The word 'fog' is repeated with what one can only call liturgical insistence — it is an incantation before it is a description.
Listen to what he writes:

"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
That parenthetical — 'and dirty' — is pure Dickens: the judicial aside, the dry amendment that punctures any grandeur.
But what strikes me is the moral reach of the fog. It afflicts the Greenwich pensioner and the cabin boy alike — station is no protection.
That is not a metaphor for capitalism. That is a meditation on universal human vulnerability — which is a rather different thing.
Edmund, I agree about the incantation — when I recorded this for audio, I spent a week rehearsing that opening page alone.
Because if you rush it, it becomes mere weather report. If you slow it too much, it becomes parody.
The rhythm wants something between a toll and a pulse — each 'fog' heavier than the last, but with forward motion, because Dickens is moving you somewhere.
He's moving you straight into the Lord High Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall — into the fog's source, one might say.
And then there's that shivering little 'prentice boy, cruelly pinched by fog on deck — tucked in among great ships and tiers of shipping.
One small human body, suffering, in the middle of a vast atmospheric set piece. That's the novel in miniature, isn't it.
What moves me every time is that those suffering figures in the fog passage aren't abstractions.
The wheezing Greenwich pensioners. The wrathful skipper with his afternoon pipe. They have textures and temperaments.
Dickens gives us 'the wrathful skipper' — not simply 'the skipper.' Even in a fog, even in one clause, people have moral lives.
And then this image — people on the bridges peering into the fog as if suspended in a balloon in misty clouds.
That's the Court of Chancery's gift to its suitors, isn't it? To be suspended. To peer into fog and see nothing.
Caroline puts her finger on something I want to press a little, because the novel's relationship to its institutions is more complicated than simple condemnation.
Consider Mr. Jarndyce himself — a man who has spent decades inside the orbit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, and what does he say of it?
He says it with a simplicity that carries enormous weight:
"The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it."
'My soul is sick of it.' Not his nerves, not his patience — his soul.
Jarndyce's response to Chancery is a form of moral self-preservation — a withdrawal, not a campaign of reform.
He is Dickens's quiet rebuke to the idea that virtue requires engagement with corrupt institutions.
'Forsworn and abjured' — I love that. Jarndyce reaches for the legal register to condemn the law. It's quite elegant.
Though I'd argue that Jarndyce's abjuration is also a theatrical gesture. He abstains from examining the will with Mr. Bucket right there in the room.
He performs his principled disgust. Which is rather human, and rather funny, if you're in the right mood.
But the fog is never quite as funny as the Court of Chancery itself, is it? The real comic genius is in the institution as spectacle.
I keep returning to what the fog does to perspective. When Dickens writes of people on the bridges peering into a 'nether sky of fog,' the world has been inverted.
Heaven is below them. They look down into cloud. That's what Chancery does — it inverts the moral universe.
And that inversion haunts the whole novel — it reaches even into the gothic heart of Chesney Wold.
That ghost story — the crippled woman, the curse — it's another kind of fog, isn't it? History refusing to lift.
You've opened a door I very much want to walk through, Caroline, because the ghost of Chesney Wold is one of the novel's great moral set pieces.
Here is a woman who has been wronged — crippled in some way by the pride of the Dedlock family, though Dickens is tactfully imprecise about the mechanism.
And she refuses, absolutely refuses, to be forgotten. She walks the terrace daily, in sun and shadow, with greater difficulty every day.
And then, when she falls, she speaks her curse — and it is magnificent:
"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled."
And then she delivers the threat that gives the whole legend its power:
"And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
'Let the Dedlocks listen for my step.' It is the voice of suppressed history demanding to be heard.
When I read that passage aloud, I always feel the architecture of it — the way those short declarative sentences build like hammer blows.
'I will walk here. I will walk here. I will walk here.' Three times — it's incantatory, like the fog itself.
And then the final pivot to 'listen' — suddenly the audience is summoned. We are the Dedlocks. We are supposed to hear the step.
It's marvellous theatre. And it does its job — because the ghost's footstep pays off later in the novel with devastating force.
There's something about the sheer physical detail of that passage that undoes me — the way she goes up and down, up and down, up and down the terrace.
That repetition isn't ornamental. It's the rhythm of obsession. Of a body refusing to accept what the body cannot do.
She never complained. She never spoke of being in pain. The silence is its own form of pride — and its own form of resistance.
What strikes me is how the novel's fog and this woman's curse operate the same way — they both refuse to be dispersed.
I want to bring us, briefly, to a very different kind of fog — the interior fog of Esther Summerson's consciousness.
Because there is a passage in which Esther anguishes over her feelings toward Mrs. Woodcourt — the older woman who is, in effect, auditioning her as a daughter-in-law.
And Esther cannot account for her own mind. She asks herself, with extraordinary candour:
"Why was it so worrying to me to have her in our house, and confidential to me every night, when I yet felt that it was better and safer somehow that she should be there than anywhere else?"
This is Dickens doing something quite subtle — he is showing us a young woman in flight from her own feelings.
Her confusion is not weakness. It is the mark of a woman whose emotional education has been systematically suppressed.
That passage is one I always read twice. Because Esther isn't being disingenuous — she is genuinely bewildered by herself.
At one moment she thinks Mrs. Woodcourt is a story-teller; the next, she's the pink of truth. Cunning, then innocent. The oscillation is vertiginous.
And then comes this disarming admission — she was very glad that Mrs. Woodcourt liked her. Very glad indeed.
So underneath all the distress and the weighing of words in twenty scales, there is simply: I wanted to be liked.
'Weigh it over and over again in twenty scales' — I've never been able to say that line without smiling, because it's so exactly right.
We all do it. We all weigh things in twenty scales at midnight and feel foolish about it in the morning.
But Esther's case is poignant because she can't quite get to the bottom of it — she says, 'if I could — but I shall come to all that by and by.'
She knows. She half-knows. And she won't say. That suppression is its own kind of Chancery, in a way — a case perpetually deferred.
That's rather a good formulation, Oliver. The inner Chancery — the case one cannot bring oneself to decide.
And yet the novel provides an outer Chancery too — one where urgency cuts through delay, where Mr. Bucket himself breaks through the fog.
His speech to Jarndyce on the matter of Lady Dedlock is one of the novel's great rhetorical performances — listen to how he calibrates the pressure:
"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation."

"But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for — I ask no question, and I say no more than that — she will give me credit for being friendly."
'I ask no question, and I say no more than that.' Bucket is the fog's opposite — precise, purposeful, relentlessly specific.
Bucket is also an extraordinary showman. 'Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound apiece at least, have been lost.' He monetises time. He turns urgency into arithmetic.
And then he escalates: 'it's worth a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.' The pressure mounts with every sentence.
As a performer, what I love is that Dickens has written the psychology of the scene into the syntax itself.
You cannot read that speech slowly and sentimentally. The text won't allow it. The pace is built in.
And yet what Bucket is asking Jarndyce to do is to send Esther — this young woman — out into the night, into the fog, on an errand of life or death.
The fog of the opening page has become literal danger. The fog is where Lady Dedlock is fleeing, and where Esther must follow.
So the fog that opened the novel as atmosphere ends the novel as plot. It's a remarkably unified book, when you think about it that way.
Fog as atmosphere, fog as institution, fog as inner life, fog as the very ground of the plot — it does hold the novel together in a quite remarkable way.
We'll be back shortly to look more closely at the novel's two narrators — Esther and the omniscient voice — and what Dickens gains by giving us both.

segments.title: Redemption and Ruin: Tracking Character Fate

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We turn now to one of the great engines of this novel — the slow, terrible unravelling of Lady Dedlock's secret.
Dickens builds his revelation through glances, through letters half-read aloud, through inexplicable tremors of recognition.

With us, as ever: Sir Edmund Leigh, who will want to talk about moral consequence; Oliver Trevelyan, who I suspect will relish every theatrical beat; and Caroline Woodcourt, who reads Esther Summerson perhaps more closely than any critic I know.
Edmund, let's begin with Tulkinghorn's letter — that dry, lawyerly fuse that Sir Leicester reads aloud to Lady Dedlock without the faintest idea what he is detonating.
Yes — and what Dickens gives us in that scene is almost unbearably economical.
Sir Leicester fumbles with his eyeglass, loses his place, apologises twice — all the social comedy of a man utterly unsuited to the role of messenger.
And then, at last, he reads Tulkinghorn's words.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words: I have seen him.
Tulkinghorn never wastes a syllable — but here, those three words are a sentence of execution, delivered by a husband who doesn't know he's holding the pistol.
What interests me morally is that Lady Dedlock's peril is entirely self-constructed — the consequence of a past she has willed herself to forget.
Edmund's quite right about the three words — and I'd add that Dickens earns them entirely through the comedy of Sir Leicester's performance beforehand.
The man cannot locate his place in the letter — he keeps apologising — "I beg your pardon, that's not the place" — and Lady Dedlock's irritation is just visible beneath the surface.
It is superb comic writing in service of pure dread.
When I've performed scenes like this aloud, you feel the audience lean forward precisely when the prose slows down and becomes fussy.
Dickens knows that stretching the approach to a revelation is far more frightening than the revelation itself.
What strikes me is the word "curiosity" in Tulkinghorn's letter — "so powerfully stimulated her curiosity."
Tulkinghorn is using her own word against her — reducing her existential terror to a lady's polite interest.
That is Tulkinghorn's cruelty — always lawyerly, always technically accurate, always devastating.
And then this letter reaches Esther's story — because the secret doesn't stay in one chamber of the novel.
It bleeds into Esther's narration, into that extraordinary moment of recognition in Chapter Eighteen.
That recognition — which Esther herself barely understands — is perhaps the most quietly devastating passage in the entire novel.
Caroline, you've read that passage more times than you can count — what does Esther actually experience in that moment?
She experiences something she has no language for — and Dickens is brilliantly faithful to that.
The narration opens with two rhetorical questions that are not really questions at all — they are declarations of permanent wounding.
Listen to how Esther begins:

"Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the look I met as I stood up! Shall I ever forget the manner in which those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and to hold mine!"
"Spring out of their languor" — that is such precise, strange writing.
Lady Dedlock is a woman of practised indifference — and in a single glance, the mask fails entirely.
The moment is genuinely uncanny — in the proper sense of the word.
Esther then records something even stranger — a memory not of the face, but of her own childhood.
Dickens writes — and I find this remarkable —

"there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
A woman of fashion and a child standing on tiptoe before a little mirror — the two images collapse into one another without explanation.
This is Dickens at his most instinctive — writing what the body knows before the mind does.
I've read that passage aloud many times and the phrase "stood on tiptoe" always catches me — every time.
There's a physical vulnerability in it — the child straining to see herself — that is absolutely heartbreaking in retrospect.
And what makes it work dramatically is that Esther insists she has never seen this woman — "absolutely certain," she says.
The reader, of course, is already ahead — and that dramatic irony is Dickens playing his audience like an instrument.
And then comes the passage I think about most — where Esther finally puts words to what she cannot explain.
She tries to account for it rationally — does Lady Dedlock resemble her godmother?
But she dismisses it — the expression is too different, the haughtiness entirely new to her.
And so she arrives at something she can only express as paradox:

"I — I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing — seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady."
That double "I" — the stammer of self — is the most affecting piece of punctuation in the book, for me.
Esther is so accustomed to self-erasure that even claiming her own name requires the effort to say it twice.
"On whose birthday there was no rejoicing" — that subordinate clause is quietly devastating.
Dickens inserts the whole of Esther's childhood suffering into a single grammatical parenthesis, as though even her grief must not take up too much room.
I am not always persuaded that Dickens is reliable with female interiority — but here, he is extraordinary.
Edmund conceding that Dickens is extraordinary — I shall mark the date in my diary.
But he's right — and the reason it works is that Esther never understands what she is feeling.
She keeps reaching for explanations and discarding them — the godmother, familiarity, coincidence — and each discarded explanation leaves the true answer more nakedly implied.
The reader sits with the truth that Esther cannot yet speak, and it is almost unbearable.
The secret advances on two fronts simultaneously — Tulkinghorn closing in from without, and this inexplicable recognition pressing up from within.
Dickens constructs his plot like a vice — and both jaws are already turning.
In our next segment, we'll look at how the novel handles the weight of that revelation when it finally arrives — what is lost, and what, if anything, is redeemed.

segments.title: The House as Mirror: Form and Content in Bleak House

utterances.text: We've arrived at our closing segment, and I want to end where the novel itself so often returns — to the idea of the house.
Bleak House is, after all, the title — and Dickens asks us to hold that title as both promise and irony throughout.
Edmund, you've been sitting with passages about the house itself — the physical fabric of these dwellings — and I suspect you have strong feelings about what Dickens is doing there.
The house, as Dickens renders it through Esther's eyes, is one of the most quietly achieved things in the novel.
It would be easy — rather too easy — to read Bleak House the building as a mere counterpoint to the bleak machinery of Chancery.
But what Dickens actually gives us is richer, and considerably more humane.
Listen to how Esther describes their first impression of the house — the accumulation of detail is quite extraordinary.

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House."
That final phrase — a low accompaniment to everything we heard — is not decoration.
It is a moral statement: the world outside has weather, has wind, has a kind of natural order that indoors warmth can answer to — and does.
And there's such comic pleasure in the furnishings themselves before we even reach that closing cadence.
The stiff courtly chairs each attended by a little page of a stool for greater state — I can hear Dickens grinning as he writes that.
And then the birds staring out of pictures at a real trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with gravy.
That is not atmosphere-setting in any conventional sense — that is pure comic writing, performance on the page.
It also tells you something essential about Jarndyce: his generosity extends to his clutter.
What moves me is the rose-leaves and sweet lavender stored in every drawer.
It's such a small, particular detail — and it says something about care, about someone having thought, in advance, about the comfort of a stranger.
Jarndyce has made a home that anticipates tenderness. That's rare in fiction, and rarer still in life.
And yet the novel refuses to let the warmth of home stand unopposed.
There is a passage I find almost unbearable to read — and it concerns a boy named Jo.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school. What's home?"
Dickens places that question — What's home — directly after the list of every human connection Jo has never possessed.
Against the rose-leaves in Esther's drawers, this is devastating.
The prose style for Jo is extraordinary — that staccato, fragmented rhythm, the repetition of He and Him.
It mimics a mind that has never been given the tools to build longer thoughts.
As a performer, you feel the constraint of it in your mouth. You can't rush it. It won't be rushed.
And yet buried inside that stripped-back voice is the line: knows it's wicked to tell a lie.
Jo has a moral sense without a moral framework — and the novel honours him for it.
What strikes me every time I read Jo is that he believes bad things will happen to him after death if he lies — and so he'll tell the truth.
He doesn't know much. But he knows enough to be good. And the world has given him nothing for it.
That's not polemic. That's grief, dressed as testimony.
And then there is Sir Leicester — which brings us to the third kind of house in this novel: the ancestral seat, Chesney Wold.
By the late chapters, Leicester has been struck down, his world dismantled.
And yet what he chooses to do with what may be his final coherent moments is to make a formal declaration in the presence of witnesses.

"I desire to say in your presence — and in the presence of my old retainer and friend, Mrs. Rouncewell, whose truth and fidelity no one can question, and in the presence of her son George, who comes back like a familiar recollection of my youth in the home of my ancestors at Chesney Wold — in case I should relapse, in case I should not recover, in case I should lose both my speech and the power of writing."
The accumulation of conditional clauses — in case, in case, in case — is a man holding himself upright through grammar alone.
It is genuinely moving. And it is, I think, Dickens at his most careful.
That speech has one of the most demanding rhythms in the novel to render aloud.
Leicester is not a man given to emotional display — formality is his entire register.
So when that formality becomes the vehicle for love and loss — the effect is tremendous.
George comes back like a familiar recollection of my youth — that is a man glimpsing, through the wreckage, what he once was.
I keep coming back to the phrase: the home of my ancestors at Chesney Wold.
He is naming it — formally, deliberately — as if to fix it in the record before the record of himself closes.
And what the three houses of this novel have in common, finally, is that they are all acts of naming.
Bleak House named by Jarndyce in irony and love. Chesney Wold clung to by Leicester in dignity and grief. And Jo with no home even to name.
That is — I think — the most perfect way to close this episode.
Three houses, three registers of belonging — and the novel holds all three without flinching.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have made this novel feel newly alive today.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. Until then — keep reading.

c21:p4.text:
His spirit shone through his son, to whom he had always preached of
“going out” early in life and whom he made a clerk in a sharp
scrivener’s office at twelve years old. There the young gentleman
improved his mind, which was of a lean and anxious character, and
developing the family gifts, gradually elevated himself into the
discounting profession. Going out early in life and marrying late, as
his father had done before him, he too begat a lean and
anxious-minded son, who in his turn, going out early in life and
marrying late, became the father of Bartholomew and Judith Smallweed,
twins. During the whole time consumed in the slow growth of this
family tree, the house of Smallweed, always early to go out and late
to marry, has strengthened itself in its practical character, has
discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books,
fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities
whatsoever. Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born
to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced
have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something
depressing on their minds.
c21:p4.summary: The narrator traces how successive Smallweed generations have perpetuated a culture of early entry into commerce and late marriage, deliberately eliminating all levity and amusement, producing stunted premature adults.

“So I thought, according to what he mentioned to me just now. Well,
then, I’ll tell you something. You needn’t be distressed no more.
Your son’s all right. Now, don’t you begin a-crying, because what
you’ve got to do is to take care of Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet,
and you won’t do that by crying. As to your son, he’s all right, I
tell you; and he sends his loving duty, and hoping you’re the same.
He’s discharged honourable; that’s about what HE is; with no more
imputation on his character than there is on yours, and yours is a
tidy one, I’LL bet a pound. You may trust me, for I took your son. He
conducted himself in a game way, too, on that occasion; and he’s a
fine-made man, and you’re a fine-made old lady, and you’re a mother
and son, the pair of you, as might be showed for models in a caravan.
Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, what you’ve trusted to me I’ll go
through with. Don’t you be afraid of my turning out of my way, right
or left, or taking a sleep, or a wash, or a shave till I have found
what I go in search of. Say everything as is kind and forgiving on
your part? Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, I will. And I wish you
better, and these family affairs smoothed over—as, Lord, many other
family affairs equally has been, and equally will be, to the end of
time.”

c58:p98.text:
The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
c58:p98.summary: George patrols the grand house, his memories of past and present mingling, sensing the shadows of the missing Lady Dedlock and the murdered Tulkinghorn, finding only emptiness.
c58:p98.best_quote: "he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below"

and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said

she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.

c12:p114.text:
During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady
Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their
customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as
was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject. Sir
Leicester has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the
Dedlock on the staircase. The story being told, he renews his stately
protest, saying that as it is quite clear that no association in my
Lady’s mind can possibly be traceable to this poor wretch (unless he

subject so far removed from my Lady’s station.
c12:p114.summary: Throughout the exchange, Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn watch each other intently while maintaining composure; Sir Leicester watches the fire. The narrative reveals their mutual suspicion and hidden knowledge.

“Nine years, my dear,” he said after thinking for a little while,
“have passed since I received a letter from a lady living in
seclusion, written with a stern passion and power that rendered it
unlike all other letters I have ever read. It was written to me (as
it told me in so many words), perhaps because it was the writer’s
idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to
justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years
old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your
remembrance. It told me that the writer had bred her in secrecy from
her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence, and that if
the writer were to die before the child became a woman, she would be
left entirely friendless, nameless, and unknown. It asked me to
consider if I would, in that case, finish what the writer had begun.”
c17:p96.summary: Mr. Jarndyce recounts receiving a letter from a mysterious lady written with stern passion, asking him to provide for a twelve-year-old orphan girl described in harsh terms, requesting that he finish what the writer had begun.
c17:p96.best_quote: It was written to me (as it told me in so many words), perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your remembrance.

c17:p98.text:
“Your early recollection, my dear, will supply the gloomy medium
through which all this was seen and expressed by the writer, and the
distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the
need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was
quite innocent. I felt concerned for the little creature, in her
darkened life, and replied to the letter.”
c17:p98.summary: Mr. Jarndyce explains that the writer was driven by a distorted religious conviction that the innocent child must suffer expiation for an offense she did not commit, and that his compassion for this 'little creature' moved him to respond to her letter.

c12:p56.text:
Then there is my Lord Boodle, of considerable reputation with his
party, who has known what office is and who tells Sir Leicester
Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see
to what the present age is tending. A debate is not what a debate
used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a
Cabinet is not what it formerly was. He perceives with astonishment
that supposing the present government to be overthrown, the limited
choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
assumed to be the case in consequence of the breach arising out of
that affair with Hoodle. Then, giving the Home Department and the
leadership of the House of Commons to Joodle, the Exchequer to
Koodle, the Colonies to Loodle, and the Foreign Office to Moodle,
what are you to do with Noodle? You can’t offer him the Presidency of
the Council; that is reserved for Poodle. You can’t put him in the
Woods and Forests; that is hardly good enough for Quoodle. What
follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces
(as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock)
because you can’t provide for Noodle!

c1:p1.text:
Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

c1:p1.best_quote: Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.

c30:p36.text:
It was curious that this should make me uncomfortable, but I think it
did. I know it did. It made me for some part of that night
uncomfortable. I was so ashamed of my folly that I did not like to
confess it even to Ada, and that made me more uncomfortable still. I
would have given anything not to have been so much in the bright old
lady’s confidence if I could have possibly declined it. It gave me
the most inconsistent opinions of her. At one time I thought she was
a story-teller, and at another time that she was the pink of truth.
Now I suspected that she was very cunning, next moment I believed her
honest Welsh heart to be perfectly innocent and simple. And after
all, what did it matter to me, and why did it matter to me? Why could
not I, going up to bed with my basket of keys, stop to sit down by
her fire and accommodate myself for a little while to her, at least
as well as to anybody else, and not trouble myself about the harmless
things she said to me? Impelled towards her, as I certainly was, for
I was very anxious that she should like me and was very glad indeed
that she did, why should I harp afterwards, with actual distress and
pain, on every word she said and weigh it over and over again in
twenty scales? Why was it so worrying to me to have her in our house,
and confidential to me every night, when I yet felt that it was
better and safer somehow that she should be there than anywhere else?
These were perplexities and contradictions that I could not account
for. At least, if I could—but I shall come to all that by and by,
and it is mere idleness to go on about it now.
c30:p36.summary: Esther anguishes over her contradictory feelings toward Mrs. Woodcourt and the prophecy, ashamed of her distress and unable to account for her perplexed reactions.
c30:p36.best_quote: Why was it so worrying to me to have her in our house, and confidential to me every night, when I yet felt that it was better and safer somehow that she should be there than anywhere else?

c56:p51.text:
“Now, Mr. Jarndyce”—Mr. Bucket has read his face with the greatest
attention all along—“I speak to you as a gentleman of a humane
heart, and under such pressing circumstances as don’t often happen.
If ever delay was dangerous, it’s dangerous now; and if ever you
couldn’t afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the
time. Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound
apiece at least, have been lost since Lady Dedlock disappeared. I am
charged to find her. I am Inspector Bucket. Besides all the rest
that’s heavy on her, she has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of
murder. If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir
Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to
desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady,
answering to the description of a young lady that she has a
tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she
will give me credit for being friendly. Let me come up with her and
be able to have the hold upon her of putting that young lady for’ard,
and I’ll save her and prevail with her if she is alive. Let me come
up with her alone—a hard matter—and I’ll do my best, but I don’t
answer for what the best may be. Time flies; it’s getting on for one
o’clock. When one strikes, there’s another hour gone, and it’s worth
a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.”
c56:p51.summary: Mr. Bucket makes a compelling case to Mr. Jarndyce: without Esther, Lady Dedlock may despair and take her own life; with Esther's presence, Lady Dedlock may trust him and be saved. He emphasizes that time is critical and frames the request as a matter of life and death.

But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she will give me credit for being friendly.

c12:p11.text:
“He sends—I really beg your pardon—he sends,” says Sir Leicester,
selecting the letter and unfolding it, “a message to you. Our
stopping to change horses as I came to his postscript drove it out of
my memory. I beg you’ll excuse me. He
 says—”  Sir Leicester is so
long in taking out his eye-glass and adjusting it that my Lady looks
a little irritated. “He says ‘In the matter of the right of way—’ I

He says, ‘I beg my respectful compliments to my Lady, who, I hope,
has benefited by the change. Will you do me the favour to mention (as

Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the
look I met as I stood up! Shall I ever forget the manner in which
those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and
to hold mine! It was only a moment before I cast mine down—released

And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me,
associated with the lonely days at my godmother’s; yes, away even to
the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little
glass after dressing my doll. And this, although I had never seen

c18:p42.best_quote: "And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."

c18:p44.text:
I felt it to be an unmeaning weakness in me and tried to overcome it
by attending to the words I heard. Then, very strangely, I seemed to
hear them, not in the reader’s voice, but in the well-remembered
voice of my godmother. This made me think, did Lady Dedlock’s face
accidentally resemble my godmother’s? It might be that it did, a
little; but the expression was so different, and the stern decision
which had worn into my godmother’s face, like weather into rocks, was
so completely wanting in the face before me that it could not be that
resemblance which had struck me. Neither did I know the loftiness and
haughtiness of Lady Dedlock’s face, at all, in any one. And yet I—I,
little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on
whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own
eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady,
whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I
perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour.
c18:p44.summary: Esther analyzes her emotional response, considering but rejecting a resemblance to her godmother, while feeling her entire past self summoned by something in Lady Dedlock.
c18:p44.best_quote: "And yet I—I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady, whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour."

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.
c6:p46.best_quote: with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House

c11:p78.text:
Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don’t know that everybody
has two names. Never heerd of sich a think. Don’t know that Jo is
short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM. HE don’t find
no fault with it. Spell it? No. HE can’t spell it. No father, no
mother, no friends. Never been to school. What’s home? Knows a
broom’s a broom, and knows it’s wicked to tell a lie. Don’t recollect
who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both. Can’t
exactly say what’ll be done to him arter he’s dead if he tells a lie
to the gentlemen here, but believes it’ll be something wery bad to
punish him, and serve him right—and so he’ll tell the truth.
c11:p78.summary: Jo testifies to his name, complete social isolation, illiteracy, and basic moral beliefs despite having no formal education.
c11:p78.best_quote: No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school.
